An enduring and mysterious question concerning every language is: where do the words come from? Big cities like New York and London are sometimes referred to as a melting pot, [[1]] the English language. As we use it, we are reaping the fruits of millennia of wars, invasions, colonial expansion and cultural developments. Take, for example, the simple word “clue.” It was actually stolen from the Greek gods. When Theseus was trapped in a labyrinth facing the man-eating monster Minotaur, he used the “clew,” or a ball of yarn, to track his path back to safety. Later, a “clew” [[2]] mean something that guides your path, very similar to how we use it today.
Another English word we take for granted comes from Hindi. “Shampoo” in Hindi means “to massage,” or, to be more precise, to “press, knead, soothe your scalp.” In the 19th century, British colonization [[3]] the word ______ the English vocabulary.
Commonly used in all industries today, robot is another word with a foreign [[4]]. Coming from the Czech word “robota,” meaning forced labor, the word was first coined by the Czech writer Karel Čapek in his sci-fi play to explore the idea of manufacturing synthetic people. So you see, Shakespeare didn’t [[5]] introducing new words into the English language, as foreign authors also made their contributions.
